title: Order lifecycle overhaul
subtitle: Scene gallery: files, state, table, chart, timeline, Mermaid and tests scenes

scenes.narration: Orders now start unpaid, and an unpaid order is cancelled after a day. Refunds are removed. The tests cover each new move between states, but not a payment that arrives just as the order times out.
scenes.headline: Start orders as pending, cancel unpaid orders after 24 hours, and drop the refunded state.
items: A payment that lands while the timeout job cancels the order
Orders already refunded when the migration runs
Clients that still read the refunded status

scenes.title: Files in this change
scenes.narration: The change touches nine files. The lifecycle module, which lists the states an order can be in, gains the pending state. A new job cancels unpaid orders. The refund code is deleted, and a migration moves existing orders to the new states. Two test files cover the change.

notes.src/orders/refund.ts: refund flow removed with its state
notes.db/migrations/20261001_order_pending.sql: adds pending, keeps paid orders paid

scenes.title: Order
scenes.narration: Here is the order lifecycle after this change.

steps.say: Orders now start as pending instead of paid.
Paying moves a pending order to paid.
If nobody pays within twenty four hours, a timeout cancels the order.
The refunded state is gone, along with the refund that led to it.

scenes.narration: Every few minutes the timeout job looks at each pending order and decides what to do with it.

steps.say: The job loads each order that is still pending.
If the payment has arrived since, the job leaves the order alone.
If not, the job checks whether the order is older than a day.
An unpaid order older than a day is cancelled, and its stock goes back on the shelf.
The cancelled order is finished.

scenes.title: Order settings
scenes.narration: Five settings change with the new lifecycle.

cells: How long an order may stay unpaid before the timeout job cancels it
How often the timeout job looks for expired orders
Declined charges retried before the order stays pending
Days after delivery a refund was allowed
Topic that lifecycle events are published to

steps.say: New orders now start as pending instead of paid.
A pending order gets twenty four hours to be paid.
A job looks for expired orders every five minutes.
A declined card is retried three times instead of never.
The refund window goes away with the refunded state.

scenes.title: Checkout latency
scenes.narration: Checkout no longer waits for the charge to settle, so it gets faster across the board.

annotation.text: Charge settles in the background job

steps.say: Fast, typical and slow checkouts all get quicker.
The typical checkout drops from three hundred twenty to one hundred eighty milliseconds.
The slowest one percent falls from two point four seconds to under a second. The card charge now finishes in a background job.

scenes.title: A declined card
scenes.narration: When a card is declined, the pay job retries with doubling waits.

steps.say: The first charge is declined.
Two seconds later, the job tries again.
Then the job waits four seconds before the second retry.
After eight more seconds comes the third and last retry.
Then the job gives up. The order stays pending until the customer pays, or the timeout cancels the order.

scenes.title: Order lifecycle tests
scenes.subject: transition in src/orders/lifecycle.ts
scenes.narration: Five tests cover the new lifecycle. New orders start pending, paying moves them to paid, a failed charge keeps them pending, and the timeout cancels only unpaid orders. Nothing tests a payment that arrives at the same moment the timeout fires.

cases.name: pay moves a pending order to paid
cases.proves: A successful charge sets the status to paid and records the payment id

cases.name: a failed charge keeps the order pending
cases.proves: A declined card leaves the order ==pending== so the customer can retry

cases.name: cancels orders unpaid after 24 hours
cases.proves: The timeout job cancels pending orders older than a day and leaves paid ones alone

refunds a delivered order

scenes.title: An order, before and after
scenes.narration: Here is the same order, side by side, under the old rules and the new ones.

rows.label: Card declined
cells: Order fails, and the customer starts over
Retried three times, and the order stays open

steps.say: A new order used to start as paid. Now a new order starts as pending, until the money arrives.
When a card is declined, the old flow gave up at once. The new flow retries three times.
An order nobody pays for is now cancelled after a day, instead of staying open forever.
The stored order drops the refund date and gains an expiry time.
Shipping does not change. A paid order ships just as before.

scenes.title: Migrating the orders table
scenes.narration: Running the migration on a copy of production shows why the old refunds matter.

Tests  **4 passed** (4)

steps.say: The first run of the migration fails.
Twelve orders are still marked refunded, a status the new schema no longer allows.
The fix is to mark those twelve orders as cancelled first.
The second run of the migration succeeds, and new orders now default to pending.
The order tests pass against the migrated table, all four of them.

scenes.narration: The API passes every request through a stack of checks, from top to bottom, in the order shown here.

steps.say: A new order request first passes the server's shared checks, which add security headers and read the body.
The session check finds the signed-in user, so the request goes on.
Next comes the new rate limiter, which counts how many requests this user sent in the last minute.
Past a hundred requests, the limiter answers too many requests by itself and sends that straight back.
So the route, the order logic and the database never see the extra requests at all.

scenes.title: Pending orders, oldest first
scenes.label: pending
scenes.narration: The timeout job walks the pending orders oldest first, four orders at a time.

steps.say: The first page holds the four oldest pending orders.
Three of those orders have waited more than a day, so the job cancels them.
The order at exactly twenty four hours stays pending, because the check asks for more than a day.
Then the cursor moves past the page, and the job reads the next four orders.
None of these orders has waited a day yet, so the job stops until its next run.

scenes.title: Why the order changed with the cart
scenes.narration: The checkout holds the customer's cart, and the cart points at a list of items.

steps.say: The checkout calls the create order function and passes it the cart.
The create order function builds an order from the cart's items and hands the order back.
Before the fix, the order kept the cart's own list, so both arrows lead to one list.
When the customer then swaps tea for cake in the cart, the order changes too.
The fix gives the order its own copy of the list, so later cart edits leave the order alone.
